question: A local Docker stack has no AWS access. For a file-uploads feature the team weighs (a) a dev-only local-filesystem storage branch versus (b) running MinIO as a container. What is the main architectural argument for MinIO?
choices: MinIO's web console gives developers a UI to inspect uploaded files, which a bare filesystem cannot offer
MinIO persists objects across container restarts, while a local filesystem loses them
The S3 API handles large uploads faster than local filesystem I/O
The same boto3/S3 code path runs unchanged in every environment — only the endpoint differs — so no untested dev-only branch can drift from production
explanation: A filesystem fallback is a code path that never executes in production, which is exactly how storage bugs hide until deploy: the branch quietly drifts because nothing exercises it against real behavior. MinIO serves the actual S3 API, so swapping it for AWS is a change of address, not of code — one path, exercised locally exactly as in prod. The console is a convenience, not the argument; a filesystem persists fine (MinIO also needs a mounted volume); and raw local I/O is generally faster than any HTTP API, so performance argues the other way.

question: You point boto3 at the local MinIO container (endpoint_url='http://minio:9000'), and every S3 call fails with a connection error mentioning a host named user-uploads.minio. The identical code works against real AWS. What design difference explains the mangled hostname, and what is the fix?
choices: boto3 defaults to virtual-hosted-style addressing, which encodes the bucket in the hostname (bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com) — a scheme that works on AWS only because AWS operates DNS for every bucket subdomain. Against a custom endpoint, user-uploads.minio resolves to nothing. Path-style addressing keeps the host fixed and carries the bucket in the URL path (host/bucket/key), which works against any endpoint: set addressing_style 'path' in the client's Config

MinIO requires buckets to exist before any call, and the odd hostname is boto3's fallback lookup for a missing bucket; running the mc mb setup step so user-uploads exists makes the client revert to normal addressing

The endpoint_url must include the bucket (http://minio:9000/user-uploads) because MinIO, unlike AWS, cannot infer the bucket from credentials; without it boto3 guesses by prepending the bucket to the host
Docker's embedded DNS refuses dotted service names; adding a network alias 'user-uploads.minio' to the MinIO service resolves the hostname and fixes the calls without touching client configuration
explanation: S3 has two URL shapes, and the failure is the gap between them. Virtual-hosted style turns every bucket into a DNS name — viable when Amazon runs the DNS for *.s3.region.amazonaws.com, impossible for an arbitrary endpoint like a compose-stack container. Path-style exists for exactly this case: one fixed host, bucket in the path, so the same client works against any S3-compatible server. That is why the missing addressing_style is called the single most common MinIO-from-SDK mistake — the storage code is correct, the addressing contract is not. The distractors confuse layers: a genuinely missing bucket produces an S3-level NoSuchBucket 404 after a successful connection, never a DNS failure, and bucket existence has no effect on URL formation; endpoint_url is a base host by contract — the SDK composes the bucket into host or path according to the addressing style, and stuffing the bucket into the endpoint fights that machinery; and a Docker network alias can paper over one bucket's hostname, but it hand-rebuilds AWS's per-bucket DNS for every bucket you ever create — re-implementing the very requirement path-style removes.

question: A fresh MinIO server has no buckets and nothing auto-creates them, so the first put_object from the app fails with NoSuchBucket. A teammate proposes the pragmatic fix: at Django startup, call create_bucket if the bucket is missing. The local stack instead ships a throwaway minio-setup container that runs mc alias set + mc mb once and exits, with the app's startup depending on its success. What is the architectural argument for the setup container?
choices: Startup creation is acceptable as long as it is idempotent — guarded by an exists-check or the ignore-existing flag — since the only real risk of app-side provisioning is a race between replicas creating the same bucket twice

It keeps provisioning out of application runtime, matching production's separation of duties. In dev and prod the bucket is provisioned by infrastructure tooling, and the app's credentials — an IAM task-role — carry object-level permissions only: the app couldn't create buckets there, and granting it that power just to satisfy local bootstrap would widen production permissions for a case that never occurs. So create-bucket-at-startup inevitably becomes a code path that only ever executes locally — and a dev-only branch that never runs in production is precisely the drift MinIO was brought in to eliminate; the entire point was one storage code path everywhere, with only the endpoint differing. The one-shot container puts environment bootstrap where it belongs — in the environment's own composition — and the app's dependency on its success makes the ordering explicit instead of implicit

The setup container is really a workaround for image limitations — the cleaner design is a custom MinIO image (or pre-seeded data volume) with the bucket already present, removing the startup-ordering dependency altogether

The proposal fails for a simpler reason: S3-compatible stores including MinIO can be configured to auto-create a bucket on first write, so both the setup container and the startup code are redundant once that mode is enabled
explanation: The question is really about which component owns provisioning, and the answer follows from the reason MinIO is in the stack at all: dev-prod parity of the storage code path. In production, buckets exist before the app boots — created by infrastructure tooling — and the app authenticates via an IAM role scoped to object operations (get, put, delete) on that bucket, not to bucket administration. App-side create_bucket therefore has no production analogue: either it becomes dead code everywhere except localhost (an untested branch that drifts, the exact disease the MinIO setup cures), or worse, someone widens the production role so the branch 'works', trading a local convenience for a standing permission the app never needs. The one-shot container is the local mirror of the production arrangement: a provisioning actor (mc, with admin credentials) that runs before the app, is not the app, and disappears after doing its job — with depends_on encoding the ordering contract that startup-code provisioning leaves implicit. The distractors each answer a narrower question: idempotency addresses re-run safety but not the permission asymmetry or the local-only branch, which are the architectural objections; a pre-seeded image works but hides provisioning inside an opaque image build where the bucket list can't be read or reviewed in the compose file, and couples the storage image to application naming; and auto-create-on-first-write is not a sanctioned S3/MinIO behaviour — and would be undesirable if it were, since a typo in a bucket name would silently manufacture a new empty bucket instead of failing loudly at the boundary.
